image_description: A close-up, side-view of a male duck (drake) floating on water. The image focuses on the body, wings, and tail, with the head partially visible on the left edge. The plumage shows intricate brown, grey, and black patterns. A distinctive blue speculum patch bordered by white is visible on the wing. The tail feathers are curled upwards. The water surface reflects the bird and shows gentle ripples.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Most distinctive feature is the broad, flat bill adapted for filter-feeding; bill is dark grey to yellow-green.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The head and bill are largely cropped out of the frame on the left side; only the back of the neck/head area is visible.
The eye is not visible due to the cropping of the head.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Body is stocky and compact, streamlined and buoyant with dense waterproof plumage.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The visible portion of the body appears streamlined and sits low in the water, consistent with a buoyant, waterproof plumage structure.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Breeding plumage is typically more colorful than female: common patterns include iridescent green head with white neck ring and grey body (mallard), or chestnut head with grey body.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The plumage displays complex patterning with brown speckling on the flank, greyish tones, and distinct wing markings, consistent with male duck breeding plumage (likely a Mallard or similar species given the blue speculum).

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Legs are short and set far back on the body with webbed feet (three forward toes connected by webbing).
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The legs and feet are submerged and not visible in the image.
The folded wing is visible, showing the characteristic shape and the blue speculum patch, appearing structurally sound.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Tail is short with curled central tail feathers (drake feathers) in many species.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The tail feathers are clearly visible and exhibit the characteristic upward curl typical of drakes.
